title: What is Fabric Activator? - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
summary: Microsoft Learn's conceptual overview of Fabric Activator, the no-code rules engine that watches streaming and Fabric-native event sources for pattern/threshold conditions and fires downstream actions (notebooks, pipelines, Power Automate, Teams, email) without a human in the loop.
audience: Data engineers and solution architects designing event-driven automation on top of Fabric Real-Time Intelligence who need to understand Activator's object/rule/action model before wiring alerts or automated remediation.
why_it_matters: Activator is the trigger layer that turns Fabric's streaming and batch signals into automated action, so understanding its object-and-state model (rather than treating it as a simple threshold alert tool) is what separates a noisy, spammy rule set from a reliable event-driven pipeline.
takeaways: Activator groups raw events into stateful 'objects' keyed by an identifier, and evaluates rules per object instance rather than per raw event.
Rules can be stateless (single-event comparisons) or stateful (tracking value changes, transitions, or absence of data across time), and only fire on state transitions to avoid repeated alerts.

Activator consumes from a wide range of event sources beyond Eventstream: Fabric item events, Azure Blob events, Power BI report refresh/row events, Fabric Ontology entities, and warehouse SQL query results.

It can trigger a broad set of Fabric actions (pipelines, notebooks, Spark jobs, dataflows, UDFs, copy jobs, business events) plus Power Automate, Teams, and email, and does not block on the triggered action completing.
Cost is capacity-bound and pay-as-you-go only while rules are actively evaluating, and the product provides historical preview/impact estimation to tune rules before activation.

claims.text: Fabric Activator is a no-code event detection and rules engine that continuously evaluates conditions over streaming and Fabric-native event data and automatically triggers downstream actions when conditions are met.

Activator groups incoming events into logical 'objects' using a shared identifier field (for example a device or bikepoint ID), and rules are evaluated independently per object instance rather than globally across the stream.

Activator rules are either stateless, evaluating a single event in isolation such as a simple threshold comparison, or stateful, tracking changes across events per object using conditions like BECOMES, INCREASES, DECREASES, EXIT RANGE, or absence-of-data heartbeat detection.
Stateful rule evaluation in Activator only fires an action on entry into a new state rather than on every event that still satisfies the condition, which suppresses repeated/duplicate alert firing.

Activator's accepted event sources extend beyond Eventstream to include Fabric workspace item events, Azure Blob Storage events, Power BI report refresh or table-visual row events, Fabric Ontology business entities, business events, and results of scheduled SQL queries against a Fabric Data Warehouse.

When an Activator rule condition is satisfied it can trigger Fabric pipelines, notebooks, Spark job definitions, dataflows, User Data Functions, copy jobs, or publishing of a business event, in addition to external Power Automate flows, Teams messages, and email notifications.
Activator does not wait for a triggered action to complete before continuing to monitor the stream, which is what allows it to process many concurrent object evaluations at scale.

Activator provides rule preview and historical impact estimation, showing how often a candidate rule would have fired against historical data, to help tune thresholds before activation and avoid alert spam.
Activator instances are bound to a Fabric capacity and billed pay-as-you-go only while rules are actively evaluating, making the pricing model cost-efficient for intermittent detection scenarios.

Activator supports lookback periods for rules that compute windowed aggregations, analyzing a broader span of historical data than the aggregation window itself so that late-arriving or irregular events are still correctly included.

Common Activator orchestration patterns chain detection into downstream work: ingestion-to-detection-to-transformation via a pipeline, detection-to-notification via Power Automate/Teams, and detection-to-model-scoring via a notebook.
